def: Mendel's laws describe the basic rules by which traits pass from parents to offspring, discovered through his pea plant breeding experiments.
points: Law of Dominance: in a heterozygous pair of alleles, the dominant allele expresses itself and masks the recessive one in the phenotype.
Law of Segregation: the two alleles of a gene separate from each other during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one allele.
Law of Independent Assortment: alleles of different genes on different chromosomes separate independently of each other during gamete formation.
Monohybrid cross (one trait) gives an F2 phenotypic ratio of 3:1 (dominant:recessive).
Dihybrid cross (two traits) gives an F2 phenotypic ratio of 9:3:3:1.
These ratios arise because gametes combine randomly, following the laws of probability.
formula: Monohybrid F2 ratio = 3:1;  Dihybrid F2 ratio = 9:3:3:1

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Parents YYRR x yyrr"] --> B["F1 YyRr (all yellow round)"]
  B --> C["F1 self pollinated"]
  C --> D["F2 ratio 9:3:3:1"]

example: Crossing tall (TT) and dwarf (tt) pea plants gives all tall F1 (Tt); self-pollinating F1 gives F2 in ratio 3 tall : 1 dwarf.
tip: Always draw the Punnett square for the cross asked — examiners give separate marks for the square and the final ratio.

def: Linkage is the tendency of genes located close together on the same chromosome to be inherited together, while recombination is the formation of new allele combinations due to crossing over.
points: Genes on the same chromosome do not assort completely independently if they are close together; they tend to stay together during meiosis.
Linked genes are inherited together more often than expected by chance, producing parental-type gametes more frequently.
Crossing over is the exchange of segments between homologous chromosomes during meiosis I (prophase).
This exchange produces new combinations of alleles, called recombinant types, in addition to parental types.
The closer two genes are on a chromosome, the lower the chance of crossing over separating them (tighter linkage).
Linkage and recombination together explain why some traits do not follow Mendel's independent assortment ratio.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Homologous chromosomes pair up"] --> B["Crossing over at chiasma"]
  B --> C["Exchange of gene segments"]
  C --> D["Recombinant gametes formed"]

example: Morgan's experiments on Drosophila showed genes for body colour and wing shape are linked, giving far fewer recombinant offspring than the 9:3:3:1 ratio expected from independent assortment.
tip: Mention Morgan and Drosophila by name — this classic example is commonly asked to support the concept of linkage.

def: Sex determination is the mechanism by which the sex of an organism is decided, commonly through sex chromosomes such as XX-XY in humans and ZW in birds.
points: In humans, females have two X chromosomes (XX) and males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY).
The egg always carries an X chromosome; the sperm may carry either an X or a Y chromosome.
If a sperm with X fertilizes the egg, the offspring is XX (female); if with Y, the offspring is XY (male).
So the father's sperm determines the sex of the child in humans (XY system).
In birds, the system is reversed and called ZW: males are ZZ and females are ZW, so the mother determines sex.
The Y chromosome carries the SRY gene in humans that triggers development of male characteristics.
formula: Human: Female XX, Male XY;  Birds: Male ZZ, Female ZW

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Mother XX"] --> C["Egg always X"]
  B["Father XY"] --> D["Sperm X or Y"]
  C --> E["X egg + X sperm = XX Female"]
  C --> F["X egg + Y sperm = XY Male"]

example: In a human cross, father's gametes are 50% X-bearing and 50% Y-bearing, giving a theoretical 1:1 ratio of daughters to sons.
tip: State clearly 'the father determines the sex of the child in humans' — a frequently asked one-mark fact.

def: Pedigree analysis is the study of a family tree diagram to trace how a particular trait or genetic disorder has been inherited across generations.
points: Standard symbols are used: square for male, circle for female, filled shape for affected individual, line connecting mates, vertical line to offspring.
It helps determine whether a trait is dominant or recessive by seeing how it skips or appears every generation.
It also helps determine whether a trait is autosomal or sex-linked (X-linked) by seeing which sex is more affected.
Recessive X-linked traits (e.g. colour blindness, haemophilia) appear mostly in males, carried silently by females.
Dominant traits usually appear in every generation if at least one parent has it.
Recessive traits can skip generations, appearing again when two carrier parents mate.

diagram.draw: Draw three generations as rows. Use squares for males, circles for females, shade/fill the symbols of affected individuals. Connect mates with a horizontal line and connect parents to children with vertical/branching lines. Label generations I, II, III at the left.

example: In haemophilia pedigrees, affected males appear in multiple generations while carrier females (unaffected but heterozygous) pass the trait silently to their sons.
tip: Always draw correct standard symbols (square/circle, filled/unfilled) — examiners deduct marks for wrong pedigree notation.

def: Chromosomal disorders are conditions caused by an abnormal number of chromosomes, usually due to nondisjunction (failure of chromosomes to separate properly) during meiosis.
points: Down syndrome: trisomy of chromosome 21, karyotype 47 (2n+1), causing short stature, flat face, mental retardation.
Klinefelter syndrome: extra X chromosome in males, karyotype 47,XXY, causing feminized features and infertility.
Turner syndrome: missing one X chromosome in females, karyotype 45,X, causing short stature, webbed neck and infertility.
All three disorders arise from nondisjunction, where homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids fail to separate in meiosis.
These disorders can be detected before birth using amniocentesis or karyotyping.
They are not inherited in the usual Mendelian sense; they occur due to a chromosome number error during gamete formation.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Nondisjunction in meiosis"] --> B["Extra chromosome 21: Down syndrome"]
  A --> C["Extra X in male: Klinefelter 47 XXY"]
  A --> D["Missing X in female: Turner 45 X"]

example: A karyotype report showing 47 chromosomes with three copies of chromosome 21 confirms a diagnosis of Down syndrome.
tip: Memorize exact karyotype numbers (47, 47 XXY, 45 X) — these numerical facts are directly asked for 1 mark each.

def: Multiple alleles occur when more than two alternative forms (alleles) of a gene exist at the same locus; the human ABO blood group system is controlled by three such alleles.
points: The three alleles are IA, IB and i (also written as i).
IA and IB are both dominant over i, but codominant with each other.
Genotype IAIA or IAi gives blood group A; IBIB or IBi gives blood group B.
Genotype IAIB gives blood group AB (both antigens expressed, codominance).
Genotype ii gives blood group O (neither antigen present).
This system shows that a single gene locus can have more than two alleles present in a population, unlike simple Mendelian traits.
formula: Genotypes: IAIA/IAi = A, IBIB/IBi = B, IAIB = AB, ii = O

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["3 alleles: IA IB i"] --> B["IAIA or IAi = Group A"]
  A --> C["IBIB or IBi = Group B"]
  A --> D["IAIB = Group AB"]
  A --> E["ii = Group O"]

example: A child with genotype IAIB has blood group AB because both A and B antigens are expressed equally (codominance), unlike a simple dominant-recessive trait.
tip: Explain codominance between IA and IB clearly with the AB group example — this is the key concept examiners test here.
